segments.title: Why war with Japan looked different in American politics
segments.body: American carrier forces had broad rules of engagement if Japanese ships in unexpected waters displayed conduct that could be interpreted as aggressive intent. Congress held the constitutional power to declare war, so Roosevelt still needed to persuade legislators to support a declaration. Congressional attitudes toward Japan differed sharply from attitudes toward Germany, although individual positions varied. Many politicians treated Japan as a challenge within an American Pacific sphere of interest, an outlook strengthened after the Spanish-American War. Ernest J. King's later effort to keep British forces concentrated in the Atlantic and Mediterranean reflected that sense of American ownership of the Pacific theater.

evidence.note: Broad carrier engagement rules and congressional attitudes toward Japan made a Pacific clash politically different from intervention against Germany. Ernest King's later theatre preferences reflected a view of the Pacific as an American sphere.

segments.summary: Broad carrier rules of engagement and congressional hostility toward Japan made a Pacific clash politically different from American intervention against Germany.

segments.title: Why the Kido Butai was so difficult to discover
segments.body: The scenario needs a credible observer who can report the carrier force without immediately alerting it, because Japanese orders called for withdrawal if surprise was lost. The northern route was selected to thread gaps between American search coverage and routine maritime traffic. Japanese planners also treated published American aircraft ranges conservatively, giving patrol bases an even wider berth than the stated figures alone required. A storm on 4 December creates the narrow opportunity: it restricts Japanese flying while offering cloud cover to a scout aircraft.

evidence.note: The Kido Butai used a concealed northern route away from patrols, shipping, and fishing traffic, while a 4 December storm created the scenario's narrow detection opportunity.

segments.summary: The Japanese approach route deliberately avoids patrol areas, shipping lanes, fishing traffic, and other likely sources of detection.

segments.title: Japanese radar and night-flying limitations in 1941
segments.body: Technological knowledge and operational deployment were separate problems. Japan had radar research, but had not scaled production or installed sets across the attacking fleet in the way needed for reliable warning. Britain expanded radar manufacture despite bombing and later accepted American sets when they became available. Allied technical sharing and closely linked production then narrowed differences between British and American equipment. Combined with limited Japanese night-flying capacity, the 1941 attacking force remains dependent on visual detection during the proposed encounter.

evidence.note: Japan had active radar research but had not deployed sets widely aboard ships, and the Kido Butai also lacked extensive night-flying capacity.

segments.summary: A scout could exploit the Kido Butai's lack of fleet-wide radar and mass night-flying capability, though Japan was developing radar science.

segments.title: Japan's fear-driven gamble for war
segments.body: In this reading, fear rather than confidence in easy conquest shaped much of the Japanese high command's reasoning. Many leaders expected defeat against the United States but preferred a small chance won through a sudden blow to decline under sanctions without fighting. Their operational concept assumed that an angry American advance could be eroded through defence in depth and repeated attrition before a decisive fleet battle. Pearl Harbor then faces a strategic contradiction: enough success could prevent the advance Japan planned to weaken, while too little success would fail to force negotiation.

evidence.note: Fear of economic defeat drove the Pearl Harbor gamble in this interpretation. A successful attack could prevent the American advance that Japan's attrition strategy expected, while lesser damage would fail to force negotiation.

segments.summary: In this interpretation, Japanese leaders chose a desperate military gamble because they believed economic pressure would otherwise defeat Japan without a fight.

segments.title: The North Pacific search gap between Kodiak and Hawaii
segments.body: The range comparison gives the PBY Catalina a one-way reach of 2,520 miles against 2,598 miles between Kodiak and Hawaii. A patrol needed fuel to reach its search area, conduct the search, and return, so its useful radius was much shorter and left a broad gap between the bases. The command map used here shows wartime boundaries, although the prewar areas were broadly similar. American planning concentrated reconnaissance toward the Philippines, where an attack seemed more likely. Lightly built Japanese ships had suffered damage in rough weather, making the stormy northern route seem an unattractive choice for a fleet already at a numerical disadvantage. The shortage of worthwhile targets in the far north reinforced that expectation.

evidence.note: Catalina range and return-flight requirements left a broad gap between Kodiak and Hawaii. Expectations of an attack toward the Philippines, storm damage to lightly built Japanese ships, and few northern targets discouraged attention to that route. The command map depicts wartime boundaries, with broadly similar prewar areas.

segments.summary: Command boundaries, Catalina endurance, northern weather, and assumptions about Japanese ship strength created a broad reconnaissance gap along the attack route.

segments.title: How American assumptions ceded the initiative
segments.body: The phrase 'main-character syndrome' describes the belief that events will continue to move at the protagonist's pace. American decision-makers could recognize Japan as a serious opponent yet still assume that Tokyo would not choose war before the United States considered itself ready. That expectation treated American preparations as the clock governing the crisis. An opponent could instead choose its own timetable and exploit the defenders' unfinished preparations.

evidence.note: American planners assumed Japan would wait until the United States was ready, leaving an unexpected northern strike outside their mental model.

segments.summary: American planners behaved as though Japan would wait until the United States was ready, an assumption that made an unexpected northern strike easier to overlook.

segments.title: Why merchant traffic was unlikely to expose the carriers
segments.body: The empty ocean was not automatically watched by civilian shipping. Great-circle routes carried liners and merchant vessels away from the Kido Butai's chosen corridor, and fishing boats were scarce there. Some fishing boats had no radios, while others lacked long-range sets. A merchant vessel's radio could also be a receiver used for weather reports, leaving it unable to transmit a sighting. American sanctions removed much of the US-Japan traffic that might otherwise have crossed the Japanese approach, unintentionally making concealment easier.

evidence.note: Great-circle routes avoided the Japanese corridor, civilian vessels could lack radios capable of transmitting a distant sighting, and sanctions reduced US-Japan shipping.

segments.summary: Great-circle routes, limited shipboard transmitters, and the collapse of US-Japan trade kept merchant shipping from filling the patrol gap.

segments.title: Merchant-radio incompatibility during the Falklands War
segments.body: During the 1982 Falklands War, the Royal Navy delivered messages to some merchant ships by helicopter, dropping boards with instructions written in chalk. Radio silence alone did not explain the problem: even the close-range sets used for convoy communication could fail to communicate with one another. Walkie-talkies were considered as a remedy. The sets obtainable quickly enough and in sufficient numbers were judged unsuitable. Civilian shipping could therefore sight a fleet yet lack the means to transmit a useful report.

evidence.note: Helicopters delivered chalkboard messages to merchant ships whose radios could not communicate with naval vessels. A proposed walkie-talkie workaround failed on availability and suitability.

segments.summary: During the Falklands War, incompatible radios forced the Royal Navy to deliver some merchant-ship messages by helicopter.

segments.title: Where the American carriers were on 4 December
segments.body: Yorktown, Ranger, and Wasp were serving in the Atlantic, Hornet was still working up, and Saratoga was moving from Puget Sound toward San Diego. Lexington was loading at Pearl Harbor while Enterprise was near Wake Island. Neither available Pacific carrier could plausibly make the first sighting. Warning on 4 December nevertheless leaves enough time to recall Enterprise, send Lexington out, and concentrate two carrier groups near Hawaii for the later response. Their broad engagement rules reflected a political climate in which war with Japan was treated differently from war with Germany. One proposed explanation is that memories of World War I made Germany seem a much harder opponent, while some American politicians underestimated the difficulty of fighting Japan.

evidence.note: US carrier locations leave Enterprise and Lexington as the available Hawaiian pair. One proposed explanation for differing political attitudes is that memories of World War I made Germany appear a harder opponent than Japan.

segments.summary: Enterprise and Lexington could eventually form the core of an ambush, while Saratoga and the Atlantic carriers were unavailable for the initial discovery.

segments.title: Task Force 3 as the credible discovery force
segments.body: In this counterfactual, Task Force 3 shifts from its historical gunnery exercise to an anti-submarine and surface-raider search exercise farther north. Indianapolis and the Brooklyn-class cruiser Phoenix together offer seven scout floatplanes, supported by converted Wickes- and Clemson-class destroyer-minesweepers. The minesweeper conversions make sense in an exercise built around locating and capturing merchant raiders rather than immediately attacking them with torpedoes. The cruisers' eight-inch and six-inch batteries also give the group credible force if a raider is found. Task Force 3 could not defeat the Japanese carriers, but it could be in the right area and produce a report senior commanders would trust.

evidence.note: The scenario moves Task Force 3 to a northern search exercise and adds Phoenix to Indianapolis and five destroyer-minesweepers, providing seven scout aircraft.

segments.summary: Adding Phoenix to a Task Force 3 search exercise would provide seven cruiser floatplanes and officers whose sighting report senior commanders could trust.

segments.title: A storm-covered sighting and the shadowing problem
segments.body: The imagined scout descends through cloud during the storm, identifies part of the Japanese formation, and returns before visual detection or interception. Its cruiser sends the report to Admiral Husband Kimmel at Pearl Harbor, who would likely alert Washington as preparations begin. Task Force 3 would then receive orders to maintain contact and send more aircraft toward the reported position. Once the weather clears, repeated close tracking risks warning Nagumo and triggering the Japanese order to turn back. PBYs or other aircraft might also be sent toward the reported position, although preserving secrecy would remain difficult.

evidence.note: A hypothetical storm sighting leads to a report to Kimmel and an order to maintain contact. PBYs or other aircraft could join the search, with increasing risk of discovery after the storm.

segments.summary: In the scenario, a cruiser floatplane glimpses Japanese carriers through cloud and reports to Pearl Harbor, beginning an effort to maintain contact without revealing the discovery.

segments.title: The Royal Navy's quiet shadow-aircraft concept
segments.body: A prewar Royal Navy proposal sought a small, quiet, high-flying aircraft that could observe enemy ships from above. It would approach at night, glide where possible, and run its engines carefully to reduce the chance of revealing its position. The proposal addressed the difficulty of maintaining contact after an initial sighting. In this assessment, the design was imaginative but impractical, leaving the American force to manage the risks of shadowing with ordinary aircraft.

evidence.note: The British proposal sought to shadow ships at night with a small, quiet aircraft using gliding flight and careful engine operation. Its practicality is rejected.

segments.summary: A prewar British proposal for a small, quiet aircraft addressed the difficulty of tracking a fleet without revealing the observer.

segments.title: The commanders and political systems that decide the crisis
segments.body: Nagumo's instructions favor withdrawal if surprise is lost, while Yamamoto remains able to recall the force before Tokyo's political leadership resolves the crisis. American carrier commanders have broad authority to react to threatening conduct. Congress holds the power to declare war, while Roosevelt has more political freedom to respond to a Japanese threat than to a German one. The Japanese side is complicated by Tojo's expansive reading of imperial approval and Hirohito's indirect style of rule. Kimmel could prepare his fleet and use credible reconnaissance to secure Army cooperation on defensive measures outside his own chain of command.

evidence.note: Nagumo's withdrawal orders, congressional war powers, and Japanese imperial convention shape the response. Kimmel could prepare his fleet and seek Army cooperation on defenses outside his own command.

segments.summary: Roosevelt, Tojo, Nagumo, Kimmel, and Hirohito operate within sharply different legal, military, and court conventions.

segments.title: Hirohito's war aims and Tojo's reading of imperial approval
segments.body: In this interpretation, Tojo treated the absence of an explicit imperial refusal as approval; even a sceptical question from Hirohito would not have counted as a refusal. Court convention made that dangerous because the emperor was expected to reign through indirect signals rather than routinely issue direct commands. Hirohito's reluctance to fight Britain and America reflected recognition of their resources, infrastructure, and ability to withstand a long war. He still supported a greater Japanese empire and accepted coercion or conflict against weaker opponents, including Vichy France in Indochina. Avoiding a potentially ruinous great-power war therefore remained compatible with continuing Japanese expansion.

evidence.note: Tojo's reading of imperial silence, conventions of indirect rule, and Hirohito's distinction between war with powerful opponents and expansion against weaker states.

segments.summary: Hirohito's wish to avoid war with Britain and America coexisted with imperial ambitions, while Tojo treated the absence of an explicit refusal as approval.

segments.title: How Kimmel could secure Army and Navy readiness in Hawaii
segments.body: Kimmel could prepare an ambush by moving the fleet out of Pearl Harbor during the night of 6-7 December. Dispersing air defences, keeping radar operating, and going to full alert would also reduce the damage of a Japanese strike. Many of those measures belonged to the Army's chain of command, so Kimmel could not simply order every part of Hawaii's defence. Reconnaissance from two cruiser captains and their supporting destroyer force would give the Army strong reason to act. The expected cooperation rested on the local commanders' workable relationship and the credibility of the warning.

evidence.note: Fleet dispersal, continuous radar operation, Army control of several defensive measures, and the credibility of cruiser reconnaissance support a coordinated alert.

segments.summary: A credible sighting would let Kimmel prepare the fleet and press for Army defensive measures despite their separate chains of command.

segments.title: Four decision branches after the Kido Butai is found
segments.body: The first branch lets Kimmel prepare an ambush while Washington says nothing; the second has Japan continue after an American disclosure. A third branch ends the immediate crisis through withdrawal and tense diplomacy. The fourth uses indirect imperial action to replace Tojo, opening a possibility of internal conflict or a new government without assuming that Hirohito opposed Japanese expansion generally. Nagumo and Yamamoto could recall the force before the political leaders settled their response, while Kimmel could prepare his fleet without deciding whether the United States would declare war.

evidence.note: The four branches are a concealed American ambush, a Japanese advance despite public warning, Japanese withdrawal, or Tojo's removal through indirect imperial action.

segments.summary: The scenario divides into Roosevelt keeping silent, Japan pressing on, Tojo ordering withdrawal, or the emperor indirectly removing Tojo.

segments.title: Preparing Pearl Harbor while Japan fires first
segments.body: One branch lets Washington preserve the political value of a Japanese first shot without leaving Pearl Harbor helpless. Kimmel could recall Enterprise and send Lexington out with additional aircraft for the returning carrier, then concentrate their task groups. The battle fleet could slip out during the night before the attack while personnel ashore took shelter. American carrier aircraft could follow the returning Japanese strike and attack its carriers during recovery, with dispersed land-based aircraft adding to the attack. Flight decks occupied by landing or launching aircraft would offer a particularly vulnerable moment. Roosevelt would still be unlikely to accept the risk to American lives merely to secure an unambiguous cause for war.

evidence.note: Enterprise and Lexington could concentrate, transfer aircraft, and attack during Japanese recovery after the battle fleet leaves port and personnel take shelter. Land-based aircraft could join the attack, but Roosevelt would be unlikely to accept casualties solely for political effect.

segments.summary: The United States could put the battle fleet to sea and personnel ashore in shelters, then follow the returning Japanese strike to attack its carriers during recovery.

segments.title: How an American carrier ambush might work
segments.body: Long-range reconnaissance might keep loose contact without entering the Japanese combat air patrol, though the required aircrews would need exceptional skill. Submarines are another possibility, but they offer no reliable solution to continuous shadowing. The Americans need only stay within tracking range after the initial identification, yet even that margin is narrow. If contact survives, Enterprise and Lexington could time a strike against crowded Japanese flight decks during launch.

evidence.note: Possible submarine and aircraft tracking, aircrew quality, and an attack timed against the Japanese launch shape the interception.

segments.summary: Enterprise and Lexington could strike during the Japanese launch, but covert tracking remains the hardest operational part of the plan.

segments.title: Roosevelt's congressional hardball option
segments.body: The political alternative to absorbing the first blow is an emergency White House meeting before the Japanese launch. Roosevelt could present senators with tracking reports showing a carrier force inside striking range and announce that the Navy intends to attack first. Bringing newspaper editors into the information chain would make legislators answer publicly for any refusal that left American lives exposed. It would be a dirty political trick, and secretly assembling so many people would be difficult, but it offers a path between presidential inaction and a formal declaration of war.

evidence.note: Roosevelt could show senators and newspaper editors evidence of an imminent strike, making refusal to act politically costly, although assembling the meeting discreetly would be difficult.

segments.summary: Roosevelt could confront senators and newspaper editors with evidence of an imminent strike, making refusal to support action politically costly.

segments.title: What destroying the Kido Butai changes
segments.body: Without the Kido Butai, Japan might still attack the Philippines, but the attritional framework meant to weaken an American advance would be badly compromised. The United States could send its battle fleet west without first passing through the carrier-led sequence of losses on which Japanese planning depended. Surviving American carriers would give that advance overwhelming naval air power, potentially preserving the Philippines and shortening the war. Such a failure could rapidly end Tojo's rule, with Mitsumasa Yonai and other senior figures distancing the emperor from responsibility. Roosevelt would still be unlikely to deliberately engineer this battle because every version of the trap risks American lives.

evidence.note: Loss of the Japanese carriers could undermine the expected attrition of an American advance, preserve the Philippines, and bring an early political reckoning for Tojo. Roosevelt is judged unlikely to accept the risks of deliberately arranging the ambush.

segments.summary: Loss of the Japanese carrier force could preserve the Philippines, free the US battle fleet to cross the Pacific, and shorten the war dramatically.

segments.title: A public warning removes Pearl Harbor's essential surprise
segments.body: Pearl Harbor depended on the defenders remaining unsuspecting and at low readiness. In this interpretation, replacing Admiral James O. Richardson and withholding intelligence from Kimmel weakened American readiness through short-term political decisions. The administration curtailed information that Richardson had used to challenge its policy, leaving his successor less prepared. Political self-interest explains the restrictions without assuming a deliberate plot to invite attack. A public announcement that the carriers had been found would probably make Nagumo or Yamamoto order withdrawal. If Japan continued, changes of speed and unpredictable night manoeuvres might hinder American tracking, but the returning Japanese strike could still lead American aircraft back to the carriers. The Pacific Fleet would have time to leave the harbor, forcing the Japanese to hunt for ships that were themselves looking for the attackers.

evidence.note: Public warning would probably prompt withdrawal. Political restrictions on Kimmel's intelligence are offered as an explanation for poor readiness, with his predecessor's surname garbled as Richmond in the captions. Continuing the attack would require finding a dispersed fleet despite the loss of surprise.

segments.summary: If Roosevelt announces the sighting, Nagumo or Yamamoto would probably withdraw rather than attack an alerted and dispersed Pacific Fleet.

segments.title: Withdrawal and the possibility of a new Pacific agreement
segments.body: A Japanese withdrawal could open the way to another deliberately vague agreement over competing interests in China. A new bargain might restore oil imports and buy two or three years, giving Japan time to rebuild fuel stockpiles while both sides rearmed. With no Pacific war, American personnel and equipment could accelerate operations such as Torch while the expanding Neutrality Patrol made a German-American conflict increasingly likely. If the Mediterranean war ended during the delay, the Royal Navy could redirect major forces toward Japan. Light fleet carriers developed through the design lineage of HMS Unicorn would add to the ships available for that concentration. The bargain therefore gives Japan fuel and time to reorganize, but a later war could begin against stronger American and British fleets. A settlement that looked acceptable in the newspapers could also let Tokyo comply with the instruction to turn back once surprise was lost.

evidence.note: Japanese withdrawal could revive a vague treaty settlement and sanctions relief, buying rearmament time while American resources accelerated the European war.

segments.summary: A Japanese withdrawal could revive a deliberately vague settlement, ease sanctions, and postpone war while both powers rearm.

segments.title: Vague agreements and competing interests in China
segments.body: The Lansing-Ishii Agreement of 1917 used language broad enough for both governments to accept while leaving their competing ambitions in China unresolved. In this interpretation, it accommodated American and Japanese interests at China's expense. Subsequent treaty diplomacy included the Nine-Power Treaty and declarations of Chinese sovereignty, alongside continuing claims to special interests in China. The Lansing-Ishii Agreement was abrogated in 1923. China objected to these arrangements but lacked the power to make its objections effective. American opposition to Japanese policy combined moral outrage with concern for American interests in China. A similarly ambiguous bargain could give both powers a reason to step back from the December 1941 crisis.

evidence.note: The 1917 agreement's vague terms, its abrogation in 1923, subsequent treaty diplomacy, Chinese objections, and American interests in China provide a precedent for temporary accommodation. Several agreements are discussed together, without clearly assigning every provision to a particular treaty.

segments.summary: The Lansing-Ishii Agreement offered a model for postponing confrontation through vague language while leaving competing interests in China unresolved.

segments.title: How imperial action could remove Tojo
segments.body: In this interpretation, Japan was a monarchical system of competing factions claiming to act for the emperor. The genro tradition supplied senior figures who could interpret imperial wishes and influence prime-ministerial appointments from outside the army and navy. Hirohito's postwar gift of a personal pen and inkstone to Mitsumasa Yonai, then involved in constitutional reconstruction, suggests that Yonai held de facto genro status. Public imperial endorsement of such an elder could force military ministers to choose between the emperor and Tojo. Withdrawing those officers from the cabinet could bring down the government, and Yonai's authority within the navy might secure a naval minister's resignation even without a formal appointment. Rival factions competed to present themselves as the emperor's true servants, so an imperial signal against Tojo would encourage them to replace him.

evidence.note: Genro authority could force military ministers to choose between the emperor and Tojo, whose cabinet would fall if they withdrew. Yonai's naval standing and the interpretation of his later imperial gift support his proposed role as intermediary.

segments.summary: Hirohito could act indirectly through a trusted elder such as Mitsumasa Yonai, isolating Tojo without issuing a public command.

segments.title: How a post-Tojo Japan might rebuild deterrence
segments.body: A civil conflict would remain possible after Tojo's removal, though rival factions would probably turn against him. A replacement government seeking time to reorganize might emphasize deterrence by publicly revealing the Yamato class and its capabilities, potentially provoking new construction programs abroad. A pause before the next crisis could also support a renewed effort to improve Japanese infrastructure. Mitsumasa Yonai's relationships in Britain and the United States would make him unusually well placed to seek a stabilizing agreement, even if the chance of durable peace remained small. Hirohito would not need to issue a broadcast order: in the language of the imperial court, a carefully phrased question about Tojo's fitness could be enough for senior intermediaries to act.

evidence.note: Civil conflict after Tojo's removal remains possible, though rival factions are expected to limit resistance. Yamato-class disclosure could strengthen deterrence and stimulate foreign construction, while Japan improves infrastructure and Yonai seeks an agreement through his foreign connections. Court convention permits indirect imperial intervention.

segments.summary: A government seeking to avoid immediate war could publicize the Yamato class, rebuild infrastructure, and use Yonai's foreign relationships to support a temporary settlement.

segments.title: Churchill and Hitler complicate the Pacific crisis
segments.body: Churchill would likely promise support and try to reinforce Singapore, increasing pressure on Tokyo. Hitler's belief that great powers should declare rather than receive war makes an impulsive declaration against the United States plausible even before Japan attacks. His decision to declare war after Pearl Harbor supports considering an early declaration here, although its timing remains speculative. The resulting alignment could leave Germany and Italy at war with America while Japan withdraws its carriers. If imperial action also removes Tojo, the new Japanese government might then step away from the Tripartite Pact, leaving America freer to concentrate on Europe. Removing Tojo would probably also displace many of his hardline supporters, making this the branch with the best chance of peace between Japan and the United States.

evidence.note: British support and reinforcement of Singapore could accompany a premature German declaration of war. Japan might withdraw and leave the Tripartite Pact, particularly if Tojo and supporting hardliners lose power.

segments.summary: British support and a premature German declaration of war could pull the United States into Europe even if Japan withdraws.

segments.title: Diplomatic culture, concessions, and sanctions relief
segments.body: A new Japanese government might obtain sanctions relief while Washington focuses on Germany, but cultural expectations make an agreement difficult. American officials could treat concessions before talks as proof of good faith, while Japanese leaders could read the same advance concessions as a public admission of weakness. Concessions made inside formal negotiations could instead be presented domestically as exchanges conducted from a position of strength. The difference matters especially in a factional system where ministers risk violence for appearing to betray national interests. Insisting on preliminary concessions could therefore prevent negotiations even when making those concessions during talks would be politically possible.

evidence.note: American officials treated concessions before talks as evidence of good faith, while Japanese leaders could view the same act as weakness unless it occurred within negotiations.

segments.summary: American demands for concessions before talks ran into Japanese leaders' need to avoid appearing weak at home.

segments.title: The likeliest outcome: withdrawal and a rearmament race
segments.body: Roosevelt would probably announce the sighting, and the Japanese carriers would probably withdraw. The uncertainty is whether Tojo orders the retreat, Yamamoto acts first, or imperial intervention removes Tojo after a confrontation. A Tojo-led withdrawal is expected to delay war by only two or three years, while a government change leaves more room for peace. Renewed fuel imports would give Japan time to reorganize and consider how to counter the coming Essex-class carrier fleet. Further I-400 submarine development is one speculative possibility. Delay would also let the larger American industrial base pull farther ahead, so restored fuel supplies would buy Japan options without resolving the underlying imbalance.

evidence.note: Public warning and Japanese withdrawal are judged most likely. A Tojo-ordered retreat is expected to delay war two or three years, while his removal leaves other outcomes open. The coming Essex fleet poses a construction challenge for Japan, with I-400 development offered as one possibility.

segments.summary: A public warning would probably make the Japanese carriers withdraw, leaving both powers time to rearm and Japan facing a growing industrial disadvantage.

segments.title: Why Taranto and Tsushima are imperfect parallels
segments.body: Taranto and Tsushima offer poor parallels for a force discovered before an undeclared attack. At Taranto, Britain and Italy were already at war, so detection would not create the same constitutional and diplomatic choices. Tsushima likewise occurred during an existing war. December 1941 combines the ability to detect an approaching force with political decisions about whether and how war begins.

evidence.note: Taranto and Tsushima offer detection parallels, but both fleets were already at war and therefore lacked the scenario's political ambiguity.

segments.summary: Taranto and Tsushima lack the political ambiguity of a carrier force discovered before its undeclared attack, even though each offers a useful detection comparison.

segments.title: What US negotiators might concede in China
segments.body: American opposition to Japan did not eliminate American willingness to bargain over China. Proposals available for negotiation included combining a Japanese-sponsored government with the existing Chinese government. They could also recognize Japanese control over parts of Chinese territory. A skillful Japanese government might therefore turn a temporary settlement into substantial political gains without winning the Pacific War. Such an agreement would reflect great-power interests and China's weak bargaining position.

evidence.note: American negotiating offers could merge Japanese- and Chinese-backed governments and recognise Japanese control of some Chinese areas.

segments.summary: American negotiating proposals left room for bargains over Japanese political and territorial gains in China.
